body.x: Few topics collect confident falsehoods like mut'ah, the temporary marriage recognised in Twelver Shia law. It is described online as everything from a contract with no rules at all to a relic nobody ever practised. Our rules guide sets out the contract's conditions in full; this post does the other job — it takes the claims a reader is most likely to have heard, one at a time, and answers each with the actual Twelver position. Where marjas differ, that is said. Nothing here is a personal ruling; for that, a reader's own marja is the reference.
"It needs no mahr and no fixed term — you just agree"

This inverts the law. In Twelver fiqh, the stated duration and the specified mahr are the two pillars that make a mut'ah a mut'ah. A temporary contract with no mahr named is invalid — not irregular, invalid. The term must likewise be stated and known to both parties; jurists discuss what follows if it is left out, with many holding that a contract silent on duration is treated as a permanent marriage instead, which is precisely why scholars insist both elements be spoken explicitly in the formula. Far from being the informal option, mut'ah is in this respect stricter than permanent nikah, where an unstated mahr does not void the contract.
"It is a secret arrangement that Islam blesses casually"

Mut'ah is a contract, concluded with a spoken formula of offer and acceptance, creating real legal effects from the moment it is made: the parties become lawful spouses, certain other marriages become forbidden during its term, and obligations attach at its end. Nothing in the law requires or rewards secrecy, and the conditions that apply to a bride in permanent marriage apply here too — under the majority of marjas, a woman who has never been married requires her wali's permission, a point on which scholars have written at length and on which no one should improvise. An arrangement conducted by deception — hidden from guardians whose consent is required, or from an existing spouse in defiance of stipulated conditions — is not made sound by calling it mut'ah. Scholars across the tradition also counsel openly about its social costs, particularly to women; the contract's existence in fiqh books is not a recommendation to use it lightly.

The casual picture fails on the contract's paperwork too. The formula must be pronounced correctly, by the parties or their appointed representatives; the woman must be free of every impediment — not married, not in a waiting period, not within the prohibited degrees; and a man already in a permanent marriage faces additional conditions in the rulings of many marjas, including, in some rulings, his wife's permission where the second contract is with a woman of the People of the Book. A form of marriage surrounded by this many gates was never designed as an unregulated one, whatever its critics or its careless defenders say.
"Children born from it are not really legitimate"

This is simply false in Twelver law, and it is the misconception scholars correct most firmly. A child born of a valid mut'ah is the legitimate child of both parents in every respect: lineage is established, the child carries the father's name, maintenance is owed, and inheritance runs between the child and both parents exactly as for a child of a permanent marriage. It is the spouses who do not automatically inherit from one another — a separate rule, which some marjas allow the couple to alter by stipulation. Confusing the two rules produces the myth; the child's status was never the doubtful part.
"When it ends, it just ends — there is no waiting period"

There is. When a mut'ah expires or the husband returns the remaining time, the wife observes an iddah before any new marriage: in the standard ruling, two menstrual cycles, or forty-five days for a woman who does not menstruate, and if she is pregnant, until the child is born. Marjas phrase the details in their own manuals, but the existence of the waiting period is not in dispute among them. The claim of "no iddah" usually travels with the claim of "no rules", and both fail on the same page of any practical-laws book.
"Everyone agreed it was allowed until politics banned it"

The history is genuinely contested, and honesty requires saying what each side actually holds. The Twelver position is that mut'ah was permitted by the Qur'an (the reading of verse 4:24 that Shia scholarship defends), was practised in the Prophet's lifetime, and was prohibited after his death by the second caliph, Umar — a prohibition Shia jurists regard as having no authority to override the Qur'an. The Sunni position is that the Prophet himself prohibited it during his lifetime — reports place this at Khaybar, at the conquest of Makkah, or at Hunayn — and that Umar was enforcing, not inventing, the ban. These are two coherent, opposed readings of the early sources, argued by serious scholars for over a thousand years. "Politics" explains neither side fairly, and a reader deserves the disagreement stated straight rather than settled by slogan.
Where this leaves a reader of Shia Rishta

We publish this explainer because the questions arrive constantly and bad answers fill any silence. But the site's own position is short and unambiguous: Shia Rishta is for permanent nikah only. Profiles are built around lifelong marriage, families and walis are part of the process, and content about mut'ah here is information for understanding a debated area of fiqh — never an introduction service for it. Readers weighing any of these questions personally should put them to their own marja, whose ruling, not a blog post, is what binds them.

excerpt: Five common claims about mut'ah answered one by one with the accurate Twelver position — on mahr and duration as pillars, secrecy, children's legitimacy, iddah, and the honestly contested early history.
title: Temporary marriage (mut'ah): rules and misconceptions
